report_name: FBI Warns of MFA-Bypassing OAuth Phishing

threat_actors.name: Unidentified Actors
threat_actors.description: Unidentified threat actors conducting a sophisticated OAuth consent phishing campaign targeting high-profile individuals since late 2025. The actors impersonate public figures to trick victims into granting malicious OAuth applications access to their cloud accounts.

attack_patterns.name: Spearphishing Link
attack_patterns.description: Attackers use social engineering to send a phishing email or message with a link to a legitimate OAuth consent endpoint for a malicious application.

attack_patterns.name: User Execution
attack_patterns.description: The attack relies on the victim clicking "Accept" on a legitimate OAuth consent screen, which is the user action that grants the malicious application access to their account data.

attack_patterns.name: Steal Application Access Token
attack_patterns.description: After a user grants consent, the OAuth provider issues an access token to the attacker's malicious application, effectively stealing a token that grants access to the user's account.

attack_patterns.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material
attack_patterns.description: Attackers use the stolen OAuth access token as a form of alternate authentication material to make API calls and access the victim's data, bypassing the need for a password or MFA.

attack_patterns.name: Remote Email Collection
attack_patterns.description: The stolen access token allows attackers to read and send emails from the victim's account via API calls.

attack_patterns.name: Data from Cloud Storage
attack_patterns.description: The stolen access token allows attackers to access and exfiltrate files stored in the victim's cloud services, such as OneDrive or Google Drive.

malware.name: Malicious OAuth Application
malware.description: A malicious third-party application registered with an OAuth 2.0 provider like Google or Microsoft. It is designed to request excessive permissions and trick users into granting consent, enabling the attacker to gain token-based access to the user's account.

identities.name: Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
identities.description: Issued a public service announcement through its IC3 center to warn about the OAuth consent phishing campaign.

identities.name: Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
identities.description: The FBI center that published the warning about the ongoing consent phishing campaign.

identities.name: Google
identities.description: One of the major OAuth 2.0 providers whose platform is abused by attackers to register malicious applications and display consent screens.

identities.name: Microsoft
identities.description: One of the major OAuth 2.0 providers whose platform (Azure AD) is abused by attackers to register malicious applications and display consent screens.

identities.name: Prominent Individuals
identities.description: The primary target group for the consent phishing campaign, including public figures, journalists, and government officials.

infrastructure.name: Malicious OAuth Application Infrastructure
infrastructure.description: The attacker-controlled infrastructure used to register, host, and operate the malicious OAuth application that receives the authorization token after a victim grants consent.
